h1:
Wat Phra Non Chaksi
Sing Buri's Giant Reclining Buddha
intro: Ask a local in Sing Buri where you should go to pay your respects, and Wat Phra Non Chaksi is usually one of the first names you'll hear. This is home to a reclining Buddha over 47 metres long, stretched the full length of its hall — a Sukhothai-era image that has stood here since before the Ayutthaya kingdom. Here's what there is to bow before, where to make your wishes, and how to get there.

blocks.html: Wat Phra Non Chaksi is a third-class royal temple of the worawihan grade, in Chaksi sub-district, Mueang Sing Buri district, about 4 kilometres from the town centre along the Sing Buri–Suphan Buri road (Highway 3032). It's an old temple thought to predate the Ayutthaya period. Many people come to Sing Buri specifically to bow before this reclining Buddha, then carry on to the Bang Rachan Heroes Memorial Park or sit down for a bowl of boat noodles by the river.

blocks.text: The Reclining Buddha — what everyone comes to bow before

blocks.html: The main image here is a reclining Buddha (Phra Phuttha Saiyat) roughly 47 metres and 42 centimetres long, a Sukhothai-era figure with very graceful, flowing lines. It rests inside a large hall, with the face turned to the north and the head to the east. As you walk into the hall the image stretches the entire length of the space, so you have to walk all the way to the far end before you reach the feet. It ranks among the longest reclining Buddhas in Thailand.

The temple's age shows in its history of royal visits over the centuries, from King Borommakot of Ayutthaya through to King Rama V, who restored the image and built a new hall, ordination hall, and monastic quarters. King Rama IX also came to pay his respects here in 1976. That history makes the temple both a sacred site and a place of real historical value for the province.

blocks.title: Before you enter the hall
blocks.html: Take off your shoes every time before stepping up into the hall, and dress modestly with shoulders and knees covered — this is a royal temple. Mornings are easier to walk before the sun gets harsh. You can take photos of the image as usual, but don't point your feet toward it or turn your back on it.

blocks.text: Other sacred images in the hall and around the temple

blocks.html: Besides the reclining Buddha, the hall holds several other important images that people like to pray to. Take a moment to work through each one before you leave.

items: Phra Kan — a stone Buddha image lacquered and gilded, enshrined inside the hall. This old image is revered by locals, who come to pray for protection and safe passage.
Phra Kaeo — a cast image seated in the diamond-throne (full-lotus) posture, made in the reign of King Rama V, with beautiful features. It sits alongside Phra Kan in the same hall.
Sal trees around the temple — the grounds are shady, with plenty of large trees, so it's an easy place to take a stroll after you've finished praying.
The market in front of the temple — local food and souvenirs are sold here during the day, worth grabbing for the road ahead.

blocks.text: How to pray — a simple guide

blocks.html: There's no complicated ritual. Most people pick up flowers, incense, and candles sold near the temple, then go to bow before the reclining Buddha first, settling their mind on whatever they want to ask for. After that they move on to Phra Kan and Phra Kaeo. Many come to pray about health, work, and a safe journey.

items.name: Gold-leaf and bad-luck rites
items.blurb: There are spots inside the hall for applying gold leaf and making a donation. Give as much as your faith moves you to — it's never required.

items.name: Topping up the oil lamps
items.blurb: At times there are points to add oil to the lamps and offer alms to the monks, a merit-making act people like to add after bowing to the Buddha.

blocks.text: Opening hours, entry, and getting there

items: Opening hours — open daily for worship, roughly 08:00–16:00 (it gets busy on major religious days, so go early).
Entry — no entry fee; donate as your faith moves you.
Location — Chaksi sub-district, Mueang Sing Buri district, about 4 km from the town centre along Highway 3032 (Sing Buri–Suphan Buri).
Driving yourself — from Bangkok, take Highway 32 (the Asia Highway), about 2 hours. There's a car park at the temple.
No car — take a coach or van to Sing Buri town, then a hired motorbike or songthaew on to the temple.

blocks.title: Make the trip worth it
blocks.html: The temple isn't far from the town centre, so you can visit here in the morning and then carry on to the Bang Rachan Heroes Memorial Park, or head down for boat noodles and river fish along the Noi River — all in a single day.

faq.q: How long is the Phra Non Chaksi reclining Buddha?
faq.a: The image is roughly 47 metres and 42 centimetres long, a Sukhothai-era reclining Buddha that ranks among the longest in Thailand. It's enshrined in the hall of Wat Phra Non Chaksi Worawihan.

faq.q: What are the opening hours of Wat Phra Non Chaksi?
faq.a: It's open daily for worship, roughly 08:00–16:00, with no entry fee — donate as your faith moves you. Mornings are best, when the air is cooler and the crowds are thinner.

faq.q: Is the temple far from Sing Buri town?
faq.a: Not far. It's in Chaksi sub-district, about 4 kilometres from the town centre along Highway 3032 (the Sing Buri–Suphan Buri road) — just a few minutes' drive. There's a car park at the temple.

faq.q: Besides the reclining Buddha, what else is there to bow before?
faq.a: The hall also holds Phra Kan, a lacquered and gilded stone Buddha, and Phra Kaeo, a cast image seated in the full-lotus posture from the reign of King Rama V. People come to pray to them for health, work, and protection.

faq.q: What should I wear to Wat Phra Non Chaksi?
faq.a: Dress modestly with your shoulders and knees covered, since this is a royal temple, and take off your shoes every time before stepping up into the hall.
